claims.claim: A major motive for European exploration was direct access to the lucrative Asian spice trade, alongside the search for gold and wealth, the desire to spread Roman Catholic Christianity, and competition and glory among rival kingdoms.

Fifteenth-century navigation was enabled by ships and instruments including the caravel, the magnetic compass (of Chinese origin), the astrolabe (used to determine latitude from the stars), the lateen sail (adopted from Arab sailors), and improved maps.

Portugal systematically explored the west African coast in the 1400s; Bartolomeu Dias reached the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, and Vasco da Gama opened the first direct European sea route to India, departing Lisbon on 8 July 1497 and reaching Calicut on 18 May 1498.

Christopher Columbus's first voyage, sponsored by Isabella and Ferdinand of Spain, departed on 3 August 1492 and made landfall in the Caribbean on 12 October 1492; he made four voyages between 1492 and 1504, never reached mainland Asia as he believed, and encountered islands already inhabited by Indigenous peoples (Arawak/Taino).

The Spanish-sponsored Magellan expedition departed Seville on 10 August 1519 with five ships; Magellan was killed at the battle of Mactan in the Philippines on 27 April 1521; Juan Sebastian Elcano completed the first circumnavigation aboard the Victoria, reaching Spain on 6 September 1522 with only 18 survivors.

The Columbian Exchange, a term coined by Alfred Crosby in 1972, was the transfer of crops (e.g., maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao from the Americas; wheat, rice, sugar from the Old World), animals (horses, cattle, pigs), people, and diseases between the hemispheres after 1492.

Old World infectious diseases such as smallpox, measles, and influenza, to which Indigenous Americans had no prior immunity, killed a very large share of the Indigenous population; estimates run as high as roughly 90-95 percent in some regions, with about 90% of native populations estimated to have perished by 1650.

The Americas were home to millions of people before 1492, so the events of that year are best understood as an encounter and invasion rather than the discovery of empty land, with catastrophic consequences for Indigenous peoples.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The scale of Indigenous population decline
positions: Estimates of pre-contact population and mortality vary widely among scholars
Regional death rates from epidemics are estimated as high as 90-95%, with roughly 90% of native populations estimated lost by 1650
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a range and described honestly as a catastrophe: Old World diseases killed a very large share, often estimated at the majority and up to ~90-95% in some regions, without asserting a single precise global figure.

positions: Older narratives call it the 'discovery of America'
The Americas were long inhabited by millions
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Framed as an encounter/invasion, not a discovery of empty land, following current scholarly and OER framing; Columbus himself never recognized he had reached new continents.

sourceRecords.title: Columbian Exchange
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry, full text read. Confirms the term was coined by Alfred Crosby in 1972; the specific crops (maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, tobacco from the Americas; wheat, rice, sugar, grapevines from the Old World), animals (horses, cattle, pigs, sheep), and diseases (smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus); and the estimate that about 90% of native populations perished by 1650. Reference-only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Vasco da Gama
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry, full text read. Confirms da Gama set off from near Lisbon on 8 July 1497, rounded the Cape of Good Hope in November 1497, and reached Calicut on the Malabar coast on 18 May 1498 — the first direct European sea voyage to India, motivated by the lucrative spice trade. Reference-only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Ferdinand Magellan
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry, full text read. Confirms the expedition departed Seville on 10 August 1519 with a five-ship fleet sponsored by Spain under Charles I, that Magellan was killed at the battle of Mactan in the Philippines on 27 April 1521, and that Juan Sebastian Elcano brought the Victoria back to Spain on 6 September 1522 with 18 survivors, completing the first circumnavigation. Reference-only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Christopher Columbus
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry, full text read. Confirms Columbus departed on 3 August 1492 with three ships (funded by Ferdinand II and Isabella I of Spain) and reached a Caribbean island on 12 October 1492, made four voyages 1492-1504, encountered Indigenous people (Arawak, whom he called 'indios'), and never reached mainland Asia nor recognized he had found new continents. Reference-only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Alfred W. Crosby on the Columbian Exchange
sourceRecords.notes: Interview with historian Alfred W. Crosby. Confirms he coined 'the Columbian Exchange' in his 1972 book, that horses/cattle/sheep/goats were of Old World origin while maize came from the Americas, and that Old World diseases such as smallpox devastated Indigenous populations, letting small European forces overcome large empires. Reference-only; no wording reproduced.
